Accost

uh-KOST · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To accost to approach and confront someone aggressively.

Two men accosted the cashier the moment she stepped outside for her break, demanding she hand over the store's key.

Worked Example

The paparazzi accosted the actress the second she stepped off the plane, crowding around her and shouting questions until security intervened.

Accost means to approach and confront someone aggressively -- the crowding and shouting make this an unwelcome, aggressive confrontation, not a friendly greeting.

How Strong Is It? — approach → assault → accost

approach vs. accost

approach vs. accost: To approach someone is simply to come near them, without any hostility.

assault vs. accost

assault vs. accost: To assault someone is to physically attack them -- a far more violent and criminal act than accosting them.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ac-

prefix — ac-: a variant of ad-, meaning to or toward (Latin)

root — cost

root — cost: side, rib (as in the side of something) (Latin costa)

Put it together

Put it together: Accost comes from Latin ad- ('toward') + costa ('side, rib') -- literally 'to come up alongside' someone, which came to mean confronting them directly.

Use the root in a new word: coast

Root Check

Word Choice

Accost carries a real sense of threat or unwanted aggression -- stronger than simply 'approaching' someone. It's distinct from antagonize (which provokes hostility without necessarily involving a face-to-face confrontation) and upbraid (a scolding for a specific fault, not a sudden confrontation).
